name: Bird's nest for skin (swiftlet nest)

lead: Edible bird's nest is the hardened saliva that swiftlets build their nests from. In traditional Chinese medicine it is eaten, often as a sweet soup or drink, and said to support health, especially the skin.
Adherents consume it for a brighter, more supple complexion. Laboratory and some human research has examined nest extracts for anti-wrinkle and skin-barrier effects.

paras: The cleaned nest is soaked and simmered into a soup or drink, often with rock sugar; extracts and creams are also sold. Users typically take it regularly over weeks.

The nest is mainly sialylated glycoprotein with some minerals [1]. Red nests can contain high nitrite and nitrate [1], counterfeits dyed red exist [1], and prices are high, up to about $4,300 per pound [1].

chain: Nest soup or extract taken regularly
Glycoproteins and growth-factor related compounds reach skin
angle.text: Users eat nest drinks or apply extract creams for a brighter, smoother complexion, in line with the traditional Chinese medicine view of it as a skin tonic.

lead: Edible bird's nests are built by swiftlets from solidified saliva and harvested for food, historically from limestone caves in Borneo and, since the late 1990s, mostly from purpose-built nesting houses [1]. Traditional Chinese medicine holds that they promote health, particularly skin health [1].

The nest is about 60-65% protein, 30-35% carbohydrate and about 1% fat, mostly sialylated mucin glycoprotein, with calcium, iron, potassium and magnesium [1]. People take it for a brighter, more supple complexion. Dermatological research has begun to examine extracts, including a randomised trial of an extract for wrinkles and mouse studies of UV damage [2].

paras: The white nest is common; a rarer red 'blood nest' costs more [1]. The delicacy dates back over 400 years [1]. Research suggests the red colour arises from nitrogen species in the air reacting with tyrosine, and a 2013 study found droppings in nesting houses could turn white nests red [1].

A 2022 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of an edible bird's nest extract examined anti-wrinkle efficacy, and other studies include UVB-irradiated hairless mice, filaggrin expression in keratinocytes and an atopic dermatitis model; a 2024 dermatology review summarises potential cutaneous benefits [2].

Red nests absorb nitrites and nitrates from the air; counterfeiters dye white nests red, and authentication methods exist [1]. Malaysia uses RFID tracking, after counterfeiting halted exports to China, and some countries restrict imports over avian flu [1].
